title: When a child dies
hook: the hardest grief; Christians hold it with Rachel weeping and with hope

segments.voice: Yesterday, growing old: cast me not off, until I have shewed thy strength. Your line was tell the next generation. Did you ask someone older for a story? Day one thousand four hundred three.

A small coffin is lighter than it should be. There is nothing anyone can say beside it that makes it fit. Today's lesson goes slowly, and it is fine to stop it at any point. If this is your grief, nothing here is meant to fix it or explain it away. The Bible doesn't try to explain it away either. Instead it gives a mother's voice, weeping in a town called Ramah, a voice that refuses to be comforted. Christians have kept her voice in their scripture, and they hold this grief beside her. Today: when a child dies.

Her name is Rachel. In Genesis she is the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and she dies on the road. Much later in the Bible, the prophet Jeremiah hears her again, weeping over her people as they are carried away. In the King James words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Refused to be comforted. The Bible does not scold her for that. It writes it down. Then Matthew's Gospel picks up the same line, after Herod has the little children of Bethlehem killed: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Right inside the Christmas story, there is a mother who cannot be consoled. Matthew tells the birth of Jesus with her in it. Then there is a second thing, and it doesn't cancel the first. In Jeremiah, God answers the weeping: "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD." And then, "there is hope in thine end." Weeping, and then hope. Not hope instead of weeping. King David, when his infant son dies, says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Christian funeral prayers speak of the hope of the resurrection, and some Christians speak of seeing loved ones again. Churches describe that hope in different ways, and some leave the details with God. But both voices stay in the book. The tears are not a failure of faith. In the Bible, they are part of it.

Here's the practice: hold grieving parents in your heart. Settle, and breathe. If you know a mother or father who has lost a child, at any age, bring their face to mind. If you don't know one, hold the ones you'll never meet, in a hospital tonight, or in a town at war. Don't reach for words for them. Just stay with them, the way someone sits beside a person who is crying. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or simply say Rachel's name and let God fill in the rest. If this grief is your own, let the bell hold you, too. The bell holds the time.
When a child dies. The grief the Bible gives to Rachel, who would not be comforted, and the hope Jeremiah and David hold beside it, without taking her tears away.
Your line: rachel weeping. Today, if you know a parent who has lost a child, say the child's name to them, or send one line that says you remember. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: Christians mourn children with funerals, prayers and the hope of the resurrection; churches hold services of remembrance, some offer support groups for bereaved parents, and traditions differ in how they speak about children who die.

fork.setup: you're one of King David's servants. while his infant son was sick, David fasted and lay on the ground. now the child has died, and you're afraid to tell him. when he finds out, what does David do?
options: he tears his clothes and refuses food for many more days.
he gets up, washes, worships, and eats.
he blames his servants and sends them away.
fork.reveal: David rises, washes, goes to worship, then eats. his servants are confused, and he says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

original.note: Hebrew: Rachel, the mother whose weeping Jeremiah hears in Ramah.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means not grieving too much.
what it means: the Bible gives a mother who would not be comforted a voice, and keeps it beside the promise of hope.
what a scholar hears: Matthew sets Jeremiah's lament right inside the Christmas story, so the birth of Jesus is told with Rachel's weeping next to it.

notes: 'there is hope in thine end' (Jeremiah 31:17) is quoted in the voice; it is part of the cited range 31:16–17. Confirm KJV wording.
Matthew 2:16 has Herod kill the children of Bethlehem two years old and under; the script says little children and gives no age.

The hope of seeing children again is stated as a Christian hope, with 'churches speak of that hope in different ways'; Keeper may want to name traditions (e.g. teaching on infants who die unbaptized differs across churches) or keep it general for a grieving listener.
2 Samuel 12:23 is sometimes read as David going to the grave rather than reunion; the script lets it stand as David's own words.
Sensitive day: the hook invites the listener to stop at any point. Keeper to check tone for bereaved parents.
